rv.q: There’s Ruby, her daughter: thirtysomething, gorgeous and sensuous, who knows her worth, knows how to use it, and who is desperate to make something of herself. There’s Diamond, the stranger who walks into the club: a man worn sharp and hard through pressure, he claims to be Pearl’s estranged son and wants what he feels is owed to him.
But it may not have been a great idea for her debut play Driftwood to try and tell all of them at once.

The players tap a rich seam of comedy and jeopardy inherent in Laird’s writing, which scrapes and scratches at colonialism, race, corruption and the template for disparity in opportunity which existed (and continues to exist) in offshoots of Empire even after nations have achieved independence.
Ambitious, intense and a little soapy, Driftwood is a promising debut.
This riveting tale is a promising start for Laird as a playwright.
Driftwood is a clever family drama that’s worth watching for those three performances alone.
Laird packs a lot into this play but, like Alma’s unsound wiring that needs the attention of an electrician, it’s structurally shaky and in need of a couple more redrafts.

It’s a strong script, and one rife with symbolism: the new batch of rum that makes the white characters choke, the lamp in the club flickering on and off, the idea of driftwood washing up unwanted on a beach.
Much goes on but the narrative becomes unwieldy.
However, the sheer volume of ideas competing for attention ultimately dilutes the play’s impact, making it harder for an audience to fully invest in its world and its characters.
Family and politics are successfully intertwined in Laird’s impressive and sometimes uncomfortable first play.

cn.t: Laird's ambitious debut set in 1950s Trinidad receives mixed reviews for trying to juggle too many storylines at once, though critics praise its evocative atmosphere and textured portrait of a nation on the brink of independence.
